newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE euroyen ends down bit after narrow moves.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE euroyen ends down bit after narrow moves.

text.p: The benchmark three-month TIFFE euroyen March futures contract settled slightly weaker at the end of Tokyo trade Friday after short-covering helped erase most of its earlier losses, traders said.

Euroyen futures were forced lower in morning trade by Japanese government bond (JGB) sales after a positive Japanese economic report. The key contract slipped as low as 98.98 before recovering to end the day at 99.00.

Turnover was a relatively limp 64,948 contracts, with operators turning their eyes to next week in the hope of fresh buying factors as afternoon activity waned ahead of an extended holiday weekend in Japan. Monday is a national holiday.
"We've had a bit of book-squaring and short-covering, but otherwise things are quite quiet," one city bank trader said.

Sales emerged in mid-morning trade after JGBs dipped on an annual report from the Economic Planning Agency (EPA), which said that Japan's economy is on the verge of a self-sustaining recovery, in the government's strongest official assessment of the economy in the last five years.

Although stressing that it did not want to comment on whether or when interest rates should be raised, the EPA also said that it has been two years since interest rates were cut to historically-low levels and that firms and individuals should be aware there is a risk interest rates may rise.
This report did spark some sales in the morning, but its impact had mostly faded by afternoon, traders said.

The key March euroyen contract moved from 98.98 to 99.04, and traders said it was likely to move in a similar range, from 98.95 to 99.05, over most of the next week unless strong fresh factors emerge.

One city bank trader said the possibility of further rises on technical factors does exist should the key March manage a sustained rise to 99.04. "Keeping this level would permit a quick rise to 99.06, with gains to 99.07 setting the stage for a jump to 99.10," he said.
But he added that this is not likely to take place until some strong buying factor emerges, a possibility that is seen as slim next week.
The market will be watching for U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before Congress next week in the event it sparks moves in stock and currency markets.
But some traders say even this may not have much impact, as the linkage between the euroyen market and the currency and stock markets appears to have weakened recently.

In a surprise move, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) injected 100 billion yen into the money market this morning in the face of a projected 90 billion yen surplus, attempting to push overnight call money down below 0.50 percent after it had traded at 0.51 and 0.52 percent this week.
By late afternoon, overnight call money was being traded at 0.50 percent, but traders said the weighted average was likely to be 0.49 percent.
"The shock value of the operation pushed the rate as low as 0.47 percent at one point, but demand was strong at this level, so it gradually traded higher," one money trader said.

Around 60 billion yen of three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued at 0.66 percent, unchanged from Thursday. Around 45 billion yen of one-month CDs were issued at 0.59 percent, also unchanged.
